content: Clavulanic acid is not considered an effective anti-tuberculosis (TB) agent on its own and should not be used without being combined with imipenem-cilastatin or meropenem. This recommendation is based on the World Health Organization (WHO) consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis management. Eligibility criteria for children with confirmed multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB) are the same as for adolescents and adults. These include no resistance to fluoroquinolones, no prior exposure to second-line TB medicines for more than one month (unless susceptibility to these medicines is confirmed), no severe forms of extrapulmonary TB (EPTB) other than peripheral lymphadenopathy, and no extensive TB disease (e.g., cavities or bilateral disease on chest X-ray). Additionally, the presence of mutations in both the inhA promoter region and the katG gene suggests that high-dose isoniazid and thioamides are ineffective. Children diagnosed with rifampicin resistance alone, without further drug susceptibility testing (DST), can be treated with available bedaquiline-containing regimens at the discretion of the treating clinician. For children on standardized all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimens, if smear or culture results are negative at four months, treatment can transition to the continuation phase. If smear or culture results remain positive at four months, the initial phase should be extended until conversion occurs, with a maximum duration of six months. For children without bacteriological confirmation or those unable to produce a specimen but showing clinical improvement (e.g., symptom resolution and weight gain), treatment can transition to the continuation phase after four months, with bedaquiline continued for six months. Children requiring an extension of the initial phase or those who remain smearor culture-positive or deteriorate further at six months should switch to an individualized regimen. Follow-up specimens for culture and DST should be obtained before changing treatment, but treatment adjustments should not be delayed while awaiting results. The pill burden of this regimen is relatively high, particularly in the first 4–6 months, which may pose challenges for young children, even with dispersible formulations. Treatment support is essential to ensure adherence. Individualized MDR/RR-TB regimens for children should include at least four medicines to which the organism is likely susceptible. Most medicines are used for the entire treatment duration, but some, such as bedaquiline (recommended for six months) or linezolid (often used for shorter durations due to potential severe adverse effects), may be used for limited periods. Bedaquiline is recommended for children of all ages as part of individualized regimens, but pharmacokinetic and safety data, especially in children under five years, are limited. The standard duration of bedaquiline treatment is six months, but its use beyond six months may be considered in consultation with a pediatric DR-TB expert and with strict monitoring. Linezolid, a Group A medicine, is associated with frequent hematological toxicity, depending on dose and duration. In cases with limited treatment options, such as TB meningitis caused by MDR/RR-TB or additional fluoroquinolone resistance, linezolid may be continued for 6–9 months or longer, as adverse effects allow. Delamanid is an option for children with suspected fluoroquinolone resistance or severe disease requiring a fifth medicine, with a recommended treatment duration of six months. Data on delamanid use beyond six months have not been assessed by WHO. If sufficient effective Group A or Group B medicines cannot be included in the regimen, ethambutol and/or pyrazinamide may be considered if susceptibility is confirmed. Ethambutol should only be used when likely to be effective due to difficulties in interpreting its DST. Para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS) is another Group C medicine that can be used if new medicines are unavailable or a fouror five-medicine regimen cannot be constructed. Ethionamide/prothionamide should only be used if there is no known or suspected inhA mutation. In children with fluoroquinolone resistance or limited treatment options, extending bedaquiline use beyond six months and/or combining bedaquiline with delamanid may be considered. Data in adults show that the combination of bedaquiline and delamanid does not significantly increase adverse events, including QT prolongation. While data on concurrent use in children are limited, it is expected to be similarly safe, provided careful QT monitoring is conducted. Injectable agents (e.g., amikacin, streptomycin) should not be used in children due to the risk of permanent hearing loss and poor tolerability. Hearing loss from aminoglycosides can profoundly impact language acquisition, learning, and development. Amikacin may be included in MDR/RR-TB treatment for individuals aged 18 years and older on longer regimens when susceptibility is demonstrated, and adequate monitoring for adverse reactions is ensured. If amikacin is unavailable, streptomycin may replace it under the same conditions. Children with non-severe disease can usually be treated for less than 18 months. Severe disease in children under 15 years is typically defined by the presence of cavities, bilateral lung parenchymal disease, bilateral mediastinal nodes with airway compression on chest X-ray, or extrapulmonary forms of disease other than peripheral lymphadenopathy. Child-friendly formulations should be used whenever possible, and monitoring and management of adverse events are essential. For children and adolescents with severe forms of extrapulmonary MDR/RR-TB, longer treatment regimens are recommended, as they are not eligible for the shorter all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimen. The bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid (BPaL) regimen, lasting 6–9 months, may be used under operational research conditions in adolescents aged 14 years and older with MDR-TB resistant to fluoroquinolones. Eligibility criteria include bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB, laboratory-confirmed resistance to rifampicin and fluoroquinolones, age ≥14 years, weight ≥35 kg, informed consent, no pregnancy or breastfeeding, no known allergy to BPaL medicines, no resistance to or prior exposure to BPaL medicines for ≥2 weeks, and no extrapulmonary TB, including meningitis or CNS TB.
